introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What attempts were made to achieve Collective Security in the 1920s and why did it fail in the 1930s?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Collective security is the idea that all nations agree to act together against any state that uses aggression, so that peace is kept by the combined strength of the peace-loving countries rather than by alliances and armies. After the First World War this idea was put into practice in the League of Nations, whose Covenant formed part of the Treaty of Versailles and which began work in 1920. The question asks what attempts were made to achieve collective security in the 1920s and why it failed in the 1930s. In the 1920s the League had some successes and the great powers made a number of agreements, but in the 1930s the system was shown to be weak and finally collapsed.

**1. Attempts in the 1920s.**
- *The League of Nations.* Its members promised in the Covenant to respect each other's territory (Article 10), to settle disputes by arbitration, and to take action against an aggressor, first by economic sanctions (Article 16) and, if necessary, by military force. Its organs were the Assembly, the Council, the Secretariat, the Permanent Court of International Justice and agencies such as the International Labour Organisation.
- *Settlement of disputes.* The League settled a number of disputes between smaller states. In 1921 it awarded the Åland Islands to Finland, with guarantees for the Swedish-speaking people, and it divided Upper Silesia between Germany and Poland. In 1925 it successfully stopped a war between Greece and Bulgaria after a border incident. The Corfu incident of 1923 was less successful, since Mussolini's Italy forced the settlement and the League gave way to a large power.
- *Agreements outside the League.* The Washington Naval Conference of 1921-22 limited the sizes of the navies of the great powers. The Locarno Treaties of 1925, between Germany, France, Belgium, Britain and Italy, guaranteed the western frontiers of Germany and were followed by German entry into the League in 1926, creating a "spirit of Locarno". The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 was signed by many states, who renounced war as an instrument of national policy.
- *Financial and economic efforts.* The Dawes Plan (1924) and the Young Plan (1929) rescheduled German reparations, and eased tension between France and Germany.
- *Limits even then.* These attempts relied on goodwill. The Geneva Protocol of 1924, which would have made arbitration compulsory, was not accepted by Britain. The Kellogg-Briand Pact had no means of enforcement, and the League could not settle disputes in which a great power was involved.

**2. Why collective security failed in the 1930s.**
- *Weaknesses in the League's structure.* The USA, the strongest power, never joined, because the Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles. The USSR was admitted only in 1934 and Germany was in the League only from 1926 to 1933, so the League lacked the strength of the major powers, and it was seen as a club of the victors. Decisions needed a unanimous vote in the Council and the Assembly, which made action slow, and the League had no army of its own and depended on its members, especially Britain and France, who were often unwilling to act.
- *The effects of the Great Depression.* After 1929 economic crisis made governments concentrate on their own problems, reluctant to pay for sanctions or military action, and it gave rise to extreme nationalist governments in Japan, Italy and Germany.
- *Manchuria (1931-33).* Japan invaded the Chinese province of Manchuria after the Mukden incident of September 1931. The League sent the Lytton Commission, which condemned Japan in 1933. Japan simply left the League, and no sanctions or force were used, since Britain and France were distracted by their own problems and far from the Pacific.
- *The Disarmament Conference (1932-34).* It failed to agree on a disarmament plan, since France wanted security first and Germany wanted equality. Hitler took Germany out of the conference and the League in October 1933.
- *Abyssinia (1935-36).* Italy attacked Abyssinia (Ethiopia), a League member. The League condemned Italy and imposed sanctions, but these did not cover oil, coal or steel and the Suez Canal remained open to Italian ships. Britain and France, who hoped to keep Mussolini as a friend against Hitler, tried to make a secret deal in the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935. The sanctions were abandoned in 1936 and Italy conquered Abyssinia. This showed that the League would not protect a weak state.
- *Hitler's aggression and the policy of appeasement.* Germany rearmed from 1935, reoccupied the Rhineland in March 1936 in violation of Versailles and Locarno, united with Austria in the Anschluss of March 1938, and obtained the Sudetenland at Munich in September 1938. Britain and France followed appeasement, giving way to Hitler's demands to avoid war, and the League was ignored. The Soviet Union was expelled from the League in December 1939 after attacking Finland, and by then the League had already failed.
- *Selfishness of the great powers.* Britain and France put their own interests first, and feared communism as well as war, and both were weak militarily; they did not trust each other or the USSR to act together.

**3. Conclusion.** In the 1920s the League and the other agreements gave the appearance that collective security could work, since the dangers were few and the main powers wished peace. But in the 1930s, when strong and aggressive states challenged the peace, the system failed because it lacked the USA and other great powers, had no force of its own, depended on unanimity, and was undermined by the Depression and by the selfish and cautious policies of Britain and France. The failure to stop aggression in Manchuria, Abyssinia and Europe encouraged the dictators and led to the Second World War in 1939.
